title: Australian super funds on precipice of strategic tilt towards Asia
full_text:
Australian super funds have long invested offshore, particularly in established markets such as the United States, United Kingdom and Europe. Now, as they seek to diversify their global portfolios and manage concentration risk, Asia is emerging as an increasingly important destination for capital.
According to research by the Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia, almost two-thirds of super funds (63 per cent) intend to invest more in assets based overseas in the next two years.
With the Australian superannuation pool now at $4.8 trillion and growing, funds are looking beyond their established overseas markets for opportunities to deploy capital. Asia’s expanding economies and developing capital markets are attracting greater attention.
International Monetary Fund and World Bank meetings in Bangkok in October indicate Asia’s growing centrality to the global financial system. These meetings come as Australian super funds consider increasing their allocations to the region.
“As concentration risk grows and global dynamics shift, competition between institutional investors for quality assets is rising,” says Sinclair Scholfield, head of institutional client group, Australia and New Zealand, HSBC.
“Asia’s relative economic strengths and the opportunities to diversify along the supply chain and into high growth sectors have become more appealing. We are seeing a structural strategic tilt towards Asia.”
Australian super funds already have exposure to Asian markets, but growing concentration risk elsewhere in their portfolios is prompting closer consideration of the region’s role in their global allocations.
Morningstar Research indicates geopolitics has become a more prominent factor for Asia Pacific investors, including Australian super funds, than for asset owners in other jurisdictions.
Its 2026 Asset Owner Perspectives Survey shows more investors in the Asia Pacific region (82 per cent) than Europe (74 per cent) and North America (68 per cent) are focused on geopolitics.
Asia’s growth advantage
Asia’s economic outlook offers Australian super funds exposure to growth forecasted to outpace the global economy.
HSBC Global Investment Research indicates that GDP across Asia will grow by 4.2 per cent in 2026 and by 4.1 per cent in 2027, exceeding anticipated global GDP growth of 2.5 per cent in 2026 and 2.7 per cent in 2027.
This economic growth is leading to demographic shifts. Data shows the middle class is expected to comprise 70 per cent of ASEAN’s population by 2030, boosting demand for consumer products and services, and leading to development of new trade and service capabilities across the region.
That expansion will also increase demand for infrastructure and utilities. Transport networks, energy systems and digital infrastructure will need to support growing populations and businesses, creating potential long-term investment opportunities for institutional investors.
“Asia is a powerful engine of global growth, backed by diversified, efficient supply chains with a growing middle-class consumer market,” says Danielle Johnson, global head of institutional client group, HSBC.
“As geopolitics reshape global trade corridors, Asia’s economies are well positioned to capture a bigger share of these trade flows, marking a growing opportunity for institutional investors to de-risk and diversify across markets.”
Much of the boost to Asian economic growth is expected to come from rapid expansion across the AI, semiconductor and robotics sectors. Investment in new digital and urban infrastructure will add to productivity.
World Economic Forum figures show the ASEAN digital economy, presently valued at around $US300 billion, is forecast to reach $US1 trillion by 2030.
Successful implementation of the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA) could potentially double this to $US2 trillion. The Australian super sector could share in this growth, but expertise is required to pick the right assets.
Local insight reduces risk
In the past, superannuation funds have taken a measured approach to increasing their exposure to Asian markets, given shifting market dynamics across these jurisdictions. As concentration risk encourages funds to broaden their geographic allocations, geopolitical risk and market volatility remain factors they need to manage when increasing their exposure to Asia.
Nevertheless, Asia is not monolithic; Asian nations have different laws, taxes, regulations, rules around foreign ownership, investment structures and capital protections. This can be tricky to navigate and super funds are working with partners who understand these variables.
“Entering a new market requires strong foreign exchange capabilities, custody and transaction banking infrastructure and market intelligence, informed by on-the-ground expertise. It requires a partner with a breadth of services in Australia and in the markets super funds are trying to access,” says Johnson.
Cross-border expertise
Looking ahead, expect deeper ties between Australia and Asia, with more cross-pollination between markets.
“There is a growing appreciation of the deep links that already exist and considerable bilateral investment between Australia and Asia,” says Scholfield.
Education and tourism have helped strengthen ties between Australia and Asia. According to the Australian Department of Education, 57 per cent of international students studying in Australia in the first half of 2026 came from five countries across Asia, including China, India and Vietnam.
“This familiarity is enormously positive and will continue to open doors between the jurisdictions, thanks to a workforce with ties to both regions,” says Johnson.
